1380.title: The Mother in a cat
1380.hook: a temple priest at Dakshineswar feeds the Goddess's offering to a cat, because he sees her in it
1380.carry: the goddess is in every creature
1380.tomorrow: a singer on a train platform asks: how does the bird come and go?
1380.howItsDone: Devotees visit the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, where Ramakrishna served as priest, and his sayings and stories are read and retold in Bengali homes and in the monasteries that carry his name.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Durga Puja: the goddess comes home as a daughter, Uma, then is given back to the river.

segments.voice: The offering is ready. At Dakshineswar, a temple to Kali on the bank of the Ganges near Calcutta, food has been cooked and laid out for the Goddess, and the priest is supposed to present it to her image with the proper rites. Instead, a cat wanders in, and the priest kneels and feeds the offering to the cat. The temple staff are horrified. Word reaches the owner of the temple. The priest's explanation is simple: he saw the Mother in the cat. Today, that priest, met earlier on this path: Ramakrishna.
screen: `A KALI TEMPLE ON THE RIVER.` → `THE OFFERING, TO A CAT.` → `I SAW THE MOTHER THERE.`

segments.voice: In the stories his followers kept, Ramakrishna was a young priest who couldn't treat the image of Kali as a statue. He would cry to her like a child: Ma, are you real? Why won't you show yourself? He was, by his own telling, close to despair, and the accounts say he reached for the sword that hung in the shrine. In that moment, he said afterward, the walls, the doors, the temple all vanished, and he saw a shining ocean of light, wave after wave, rolling toward him. It was the Mother. After that, the line between the image and the world got thin. That's the cat. He wasn't careless with the rites. He'd started seeing the Goddess everywhere, so feeding a hungry cat was feeding her. Here the two streams meet in one person. The accounts say he later took up Vaishnava devotion too, and for a time lived in the mood of Radha, longing for Krishna, the way Chaitanya's followers describe. A Shakta priest of Kali, weeping for Krishna. That's the Shakta teaching at its plainest: the Goddess isn't only in the shrine; she is in every creature. It's one reason many Hindu homes set out a little food for animals and birds before the family eats, one of the old daily offerings, bhuta yajna, the offering to living beings. Ramakrishna took it all the way. Once he'd seen her, he found her in a cat.
screen: `MA, ARE YOU REAL?` · `AN OCEAN OF LIGHT` · `THE MOTHER IN A CAT` · `SHE IS IN EVERY CREATURE`

segments.voice: Rest your eyes on one ordinary thing near you, a plant, a cup, an animal, your own hand, and look at it as if it might be more than it seems, the way you'd look at someone you love who's asleep. Then close your eyes and breathe; if you pray, greet God there, by whatever name you use. And if despair ever comes close for you, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

1381.title: The bird in the cage
1381.hook: a wandering singer with a one-stringed instrument asks where the bird in the cage comes from
1381.carry: the Lord sits in every heart, whatever the caste
1381.tomorrow: why are thousands walking in the rain to one small town?
1381.howItsDone: Bauls travel and sing at village fairs, on trains and at gatherings, accompanying themselves on the one-stringed ektara, and their songs, including Lalon's, are sung widely in Bengal.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the goddess is in every creature: Ramakrishna, a priest of Kali, saw the Mother in a cat, and wept for Krishna too.
screen: `THE GODDESS IS IN EVERY CREATURE.`

segments.voice: One string, one note, over and over. On a train platform in rural Bengal, or at a village fair, a singer in a patched saffron robe, hair tied up, holds an instrument with a single string stretched over a gourd, plucks it, and starts to sing. The song is a riddle. There's a strange bird inside the cage, he sings, and I can't tell how it comes and goes. If I could catch it, I'd tie it with the chains of my mind. Our last day in Bengal: the wandering singers called Bauls.
screen: `A SINGER WITH ONE STRING.` → `A BIRD IN THE CAGE.` → `HOW DOES IT COME AND GO?`

segments.voice: That song, in paraphrase, is Lalon's, a Baul singer remembered for songs like it. The cage is the body. The bird is something living inside it that the singer can feel but can't see or hold. In songs like this, God isn't looked for mainly in temples or books. The Bauls sing of the moner manush, the person of the heart: the one you're looking for is already inside you, closer than your own breath, and you keep missing him. That's why the songs are riddles. You can't point straight at something that close. The Bauls also show where Bengal's streams run into each other. Some of their songs borrow the love of Radha and Krishna from the Vaishnava stream, and some readers hear Sufi Muslim devotion in them too. Caste had a first, gentle answer early on this path; here a singer meets it with a riddle. Lalon, in another song, says, in paraphrase: everyone asks what Lalon's caste is, and Lalon says he's never seen what caste looks like. Some wear one kind of prayer beads and some another, he sings, and so people say they're different. The singer won't stand inside the lines people draw. And under the riddle sits a plain Hindu teaching: the Gita says the Lord dwells in the heart of every being. If he sits in every heart, no caste line can tell you where he isn't. Six days in Bengal, and the streams meet in a song.
screen: `THE BIRD IN THE CAGE` · `THE PERSON OF THE HEART` · `THE LORD IN EVERY HEART` · `NO CASTE THE SINGER CAN SEE`

segments.voice: Feel the body, its edges, its weight, the breath moving: that's the cage, and it's a good one. Now notice what's alive in it that you can't quite point to, the one who's noticing, and don't try to catch it; keep it company, the way you'd sit quietly near a bird so it won't fly off. If you pray, you can greet God as the person of the heart, closer than the breath.

1382.title: The road to Pandharpur
1382.hook: a wet road out of Alandi, white caps and saffron flags, cymbals that don't stop for the rain: the Varkaris are walking to Pandharpur
1382.carry: the wari: the walking and singing are the worship
1382.tomorrow: why does Vitthal stand on a brick, hands on hips?
1382.howItsDone: Varkaris walk to Pandharpur in singing groups called dindis, carrying flags and tulsi, singing the abhangs of their saints along the way.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord sits in every heart, whatever the caste: the Bauls' bird in the cage, the person of the heart.
screen: `THE LORD SITS IN EVERY HEART, WHATEVER THE CASTE.`

segments.voice: The road out of Alandi is wet, and it's moving. Men in white, small saffron flags over their shoulders. Women with tulsi plants in brass pots balanced on their heads. Cymbals keeping a beat that doesn't stop for the rain. Nobody here is in a hurry, and nobody is standing still. They're walking toward Pandharpur, a temple town in Maharashtra, to stand before the god they call Vitthal. This is Maharashtra's Varkari tradition, and this week i walk with it.
screen: `A WET ROAD OUT OF ALANDI.` → `FLAGS, TULSI, CYMBALS.` → `ALL WALKING TO PANDHARPUR.`

segments.voice: Varkaris call the pilgrimage the wari, and a Varkari is someone who keeps it, who goes again and again. So it isn't a visit. It's a walk, kept up across a life. The arriving matters, but so does every step, and the songs sung on the road are part of the worship, not something to pass the time. Year three gave you the saints of this road as stories: Jnaneshwar, the outcast boy who opened the Gita in Marathi; Namdev, whose bowl of milk Vitthal drank; Tukaram, whose sunk notebooks came back up from the river. To Varkaris, those saints aren't only people in old books. They went first, and they're still on the road. The walkers don't go as scattered strangers, either. They go in dindis, singing groups, each with its own flag and its own leader keeping the song going. Someone who sets out alone is folded into a dindi and its music: you eat with them, sleep near them, and sing their verses until they're yours. And there's no single gate you pass to become a Varkari, no exam. Tradition speaks of the name of Vitthal on the lips, a necklace of tulsi beads at the throat, and the road under the feet. The temple is at the end. But for the length of the wari, the road itself is where the god is sung. That's bhakti, devotion, as a habit of the feet: you keep coming back, singing with your group, and the coming back is the worship.
screen: `A WALK, NOT A VISIT` · `THE SAINTS WENT FIRST` · `SINGING IN A DINDI` · `COMING BACK IS THE WORSHIP`

segments.voice: Press both feet gently into the floor and feel the weight of you carried down into the ground. Then walk, in your mind, one road you've walked many times, to school, to work, to a parent's door, one step for each breath. If you pray, you can carry a name you use for God along that road, the way the Varkaris carry Vitthal's.

1383.title: Pundalik's brick
1383.hook: a knock at the door while a son is washing his parents' feet, and a brick tossed out for God to stand on
1383.carry: serving your parents is serving God
1383.tomorrow: why would an old man call a god 'mother'?
1383.howItsDone: Varkaris retell the story of Pundalik, and pilgrims at Pandharpur visit his shrine as well as Vitthal's, the god who stands on a brick with hands on hips.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road itself: the wari, where the walking and singing are the worship.
screen: `THE WARI: THE WALKING AND SINGING ARE THE WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: There's a knock at the door. The young man inside doesn't get up. He's kneeling by his old father and mother, washing their feet, and his hands are busy. The visitor, the story says, is God himself, come all the way from far off to see him. Without leaving his parents, the young man reaches for the nearest thing, a brick, tosses it out through the doorway, and says: please, stand on this, and wait. I'll be with you when I'm done. That's Pundalik. And that brick is why Vitthal stands the way he does.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `A SON WASHING HIS PARENTS' FEET.` → `A BRICK TOSSED OUT.`

segments.voice: Varkaris tell it like this. Pundalik, in some tellings, wasn't always a good son. He had neglected his parents, until something turned him around, and from then on he served them with his whole heart. That service is what draws God to Pandharpur. Krishna, the story says, comes looking for him, because a devotion like that is worth the journey. And Pundalik makes him wait. A listener might expect everything to be dropped when God arrives. Here, the son finishes caring for his parents first, and the god of the story doesn't mind. He steps onto the brick, puts his hands on his hips, and waits. That's the shape of Vitthal's image at Pandharpur: standing on a brick, hands on hips, patient. Varkaris say he's still standing there, still waiting, for Pundalik and for everyone who comes after. So where is God found? Not only at a shrine. In a basin of water and two tired old pairs of feet. Pundalik doesn't choose between serving his parents and loving God. To him the serving is the loving, and God agrees by waiting. It's an old Hindu teaching, not a one-off. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends students home with: let your mother be a god to you; let your father be a god to you. Pundalik lived it, and the god of Pandharpur still stands on the brick, saying: take your time, I'm here.
screen: `PUNDALIK SERVES HIS PARENTS` · `GOD ARRIVES, AND WAITS` · `STANDING ON A BRICK, HANDS ON HIPS` · `LET YOUR MOTHER BE A GOD TO YOU`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you look after, or someone who once looked after you: their hands, their feet, the way they move when they're tired. Picture one small thing you do for them, setting down a glass of water, helping with a coat, and stay with it slowly. If you pray, you can let that small act be your prayer, the way it was for Pundalik.

1384.title: Vithu mauli: God as mother
1384.hook: a man with a gray beard, soaked from the rain, calls the god he's walking to 'mother'

screen: `SERVING YOUR PARENTS IS SERVING GOD.`

segments.voice: A man with a gray beard, soaked from the rain, stops at the side of the road to tie his sandal. When he stands up again, he lifts his arms and calls out, not to a friend, but to the god at the end of the road. And the word he uses is mother. Vithu mauli. Vitthal, mother. Nobody around him finds that strange. The god he's walking toward is shown as a man standing on a brick, and here is an old man calling him mother. Today, the names Varkaris give their god, and why one of them is mother.
screen: `A GRAY BEARD IN THE RAIN.` → `HE CALLS OUT: MOTHER.` → `VITHU MAULI.`

segments.voice: The god of Pandharpur has more than one name, and each is a different way of coming close. Vitthal is the name on the temple. Vithoba adds a touch of affection, the way a family turns a name into a nickname. Pandurang is another, and Varkaris hear in all of them the same god, a form of Krishna, standing on his brick. Then there's mauli. In Marathi it's a tender word for mother, and Varkari songs use it for Vitthal. Why mother, for a god shown as a man? Because you don't need to be worthy to run to a mother. You don't need the right words or the right clothes. You come tired, wet and hungry, and she takes you in. In songs tradition gives to Namdev and Tukaram, the singer calls out to Vitthal this way, as a child calls a mother, without ceremony. And the word doesn't stop with God. Varkaris call Jnaneshwar mauli too, and the cry Jnanoba Mauli rises from the road. On the road, pilgrims call one another mauli. A stranger offering you tea is mauli. The person whose feet you bow to is mauli. So one tender word runs from the god, to the saint, to the person walking next to you. That's the heart of bhakti: you come close to God the way a child comes to a mother, and if the god at the end of the road is a mother, then the people on the road with you are family.

1385.title: The saints' sandals
1385.hook: a silver palanquin in a sea of white caps, and inside it, a pair of sandals
1385.carry: a teacher's sandals carry the teacher
1385.tomorrow: who took the handle of a servant's grindstone?
1385.howItsDone: On the wari, palanquins carrying the padukas of Jnaneshwar from Alandi and Tukaram from Dehu lead the singing dindis to Pandharpur, with ringan circles held along the way.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, God is mother, so the walkers are family: one tender word, mauli, passed from god to saint to stranger.
screen: `GOD IS MOTHER, SO THE WALKERS ARE FAMILY.`

segments.voice: A palanquin is coming down the road, decorated and gleaming, carried on shoulders and pulled along in the middle of an enormous crowd. People press close just to touch it. Some bow as it passes. Some are crying. A child is lifted up to see. And inside, on a cushion, under flowers, is a pair of sandals. No king, no image, no person. Just sandals. To the crowd, that's not an empty seat at all. Today, the palkhi, and who is riding in it.
screen: `A PALANQUIN IN THE CROWD.` → `PEOPLE PRESS TO TOUCH IT.` → `INSIDE: A PAIR OF SANDALS.`

segments.voice: A palkhi is a palanquin, and on the wari the great palkhis carry the padukas, the sandals, of the saints. One sets out from Alandi with Jnaneshwar's padukas. Another sets out from Dehu, Tukaram's village, with his. Others come from the towns of other saints, and the dindis walk with them, in order, singing. Why sandals? In Hindu traditions, the feet of a teacher are honored, and sandals stand for the feet, for the one who walked in them. It's an old idea: in the Ramayana, Bharata sets Rama's sandals on the throne and rules in his name. Bowing to a guru's sandals is bowing to the guru. So the padukas aren't a souvenir. The walkers are walking with Jnaneshwar. And tradition goes further. Varkaris speak of Jnaneshwar's samadhi at Alandi as a living one: tradition says he sat down in a chamber there, still alive, and was sealed in, and that he is still present. So when his palkhi leaves Alandi, the saint himself is going on pilgrimage, again, to the god he sang to. You're walking beside Jnaneshwar, or Tukaram, the way their first friends did. The saints aren't behind glass. They're on the road, carried on people's shoulders. At open grounds along the way, the walkers form a great circle called a ringan, and a horse runs around it, a horse tradition links to the saint. People wait for the dust it kicks up and touch it to their foreheads. Even the dust is a blessing, because the saint passed by.
screen: `THE SAINTS' SANDALS IN A PALANQUIN` · `SANDALS STAND FOR THE FEET` · `RAMA'S SANDALS ON THE THRONE` · `THE RINGAN AND ITS DUST`

segments.voice: Sit tall and bring to mind someone who walked ahead of you and taught you something you still use: a prayer, a recipe, how to keep going. Picture their feet, the shoes they wore most. Then bow your head a little, the way people bow to a teacher's feet, and let it be thanks. If you pray, bow to your teacher, or to God, the first teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a teacher's sandals carry the teacher: the saints' padukas in a palanquin, walking with the crowd.

segments.voice: It's still dark. A woman sits at a grinding stone, the heavy round kind turned by hand, and the grain goes in a little at a time. It's slow work, and to keep the rhythm she sings. That's Janabai, remembered as a servant in Namdev's household. The story Varkaris tell about her is that one morning, when the work was too much, Vitthal himself sat down beside her and took the handle, and the two of them turned the stone together while she sang. Today, the songs of the road, and who was allowed to sing them.
screen: `A GRINDING STONE BEFORE DAWN.` → `JANABAI, SINGING.` → `GOD TAKES THE HANDLE.`

segments.voice: The songs the Varkaris sing on the road are called abhangs: short verses in Marathi, made to be sung with cymbals and a drum, in call and answer. One voice leads, the dindi answers, and the line goes round and round until the whole group is carrying it. Now look at who made them. Jnaneshwar was born to a family the village had cast out. Namdev was from a family of tailors. Tukaram kept a grocery. And Janabai, by tradition, ground grain and carried water in someone else's house. Her songs speak to Vitthal with startling closeness; some tell him he's late, some call him mother, and the grinding-stone story says he answered by working beside her. Then there's Chokhamela. Tradition remembers him as a Mahar, from a community kept outside the temple, so he sang to Vitthal from beyond its walls. Some of his songs ask, plainly, why the body others call impure should be shut out, when it holds the same God. His abhangs are still sung on the road. So the songs that carry the walk were made, in good part, by people who could not have stood in front of a priest and been heard. On the road, their voices lead the singing. That's the bhakti saints' teaching: love for God doesn't wait on birth or learning, and work done singing to God is worship. Janabai's grain counts. The week began with a cat in Bengal and ends at a grindstone.
screen: `ABHANGS: SONGS FOR WALKING` · `JANABAI AT THE GRINDSTONE` · `CHOKHAMELA OUTSIDE THE WALLS` · `BHAKTI BELONGS TO EVERYONE`

segments.voice: Feel the rhythm of one plain, repeated job you do, washing dishes, folding laundry, typing, driving, and breathe in that rhythm slowly, as if the job were a song. If a line of a song you love comes to you, let it hum quietly inside. If you pray, you can imagine, as Janabai's story does, that you aren't doing that job alone.
